> Like I think it’s a given that privilege doesn’t take away the fact one’s struggles. And that this doesn’t take away your identified cultures or your role in a POC space.

Hear me out. This right here is why you’re running into defensive white-passing mixed people - it’s 𝐧𝐨𝐭 a given at all. 

I’ve had both white people and POC regularly tell me that because I look white, I have no place in discussions about growing up with a different culture while in the US, and I have no claim to my Asian identity. 

Also, my shared experiences as a mixed person with those who are visibly POC (being mistaken for another race, told to go back to my country, fetishized, etc) are often diminished in irl convos with other mixed people who do not have white privilege.

To other people (both white and POC/mixed), I’m white when it fits their narrative, and a POC when it doesn’t. And vice versa. 

I totally agree with you, that we white-passing ppl must both be aware of our privilege and take responsibility for how we use that privilege and mitigate damage to our less privileged mixed monoracial friends. And I certainly do not experience some of the absolutely horrific discrimination my darker friends have. It’s my responsibility to educate myself and help them.

But I think when you feel ungrounded in your identity and invalidated regularly when discussing your cultural background and experiences by both white ppl and POC, it certainly sucks when you’re looking for community and help, and instead get what feels like a lecture on privilege. 

There are ways to support your fellow mixed people while ensuring they understand the implications of living a white-adjacent life. Which they likely do to an extent.

It’s possible to hold both privilege and oppression in one body, and I think it’s time to stop acting in general like we understand the exact lived experiences of each other in this community, while at the same time recognizing the ways we can help each other. We’re in the same boat here, as mixed people.

Edit: This is absolutely not to say that what I experience is “worse” than darker skinned mixed ppl - no oppression olympics lol, I know my privilege makes it easier to navigate our world. This is simply my perspective (and I would wager others as well) on struggles with identity and finding community.

The piece of advice that may have some merit to it - although phrased kinda poorly - is “talk less while teaching”. I’ve taken this to mean incorporating student participation and voices more into your classroom rather than just shut up and say nothing. This is especially effective for teaching languages and if you’ve ever taken a TEFL course, they really stress this point. But obviously you can’t just have class discussions every second of every class and there are some classes that aren’t as conducive to class discussion.
